The manufacturer’s recommended refrigerant charge for the asset or system, often measured in pounds or kilograms. The manufacturer specifies the charge in the refrigerant circuit and if the service technician notices that the charge is low, refrigerant is added until the refrigerant charge is at the manufacturer recommended level. 7 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. h. Note “yes” if the system is factory-sealed. Small appliances such as refrigerators, dehumidifiers, window air conditioners, ice makers, freezers, and water coolers are factory-sealed systems. These systems often indicate the refrigerant type and sometimes indicate the amount of refrigerant charge in the system. These systems are often not repairable and cannot be recharged. In many cases, special procedures need to be followed to dispose of this equipment. Figure 3. Example of a permanent trackable asset tag in a school district. Credit: Paul Torcellini, NLR Step 4. Develop a Refrigerant Charge Maintenance Inventory Step 4 is the core of the refrigerant tracking process. It describes maintenance functions during which facility employees or contractors check the equipment refrigerant charge and perform maintenance if the charge is incorrect. In many cases, refrigerant is only checked when equipment is malfunctioning. If the refrigerant can be recharged, maintenance personnel can add refrigerant during regular servicing and make a note of it in Table 3. In addition, equipment can be routinely checked and a maintenance record created for each piece of equipment. For equipment that cannot be repaired, workers can make a note in Table 3, dispose of the asset appropriately,9 purchase a new one, and add it to the inventory. This is an opportunity to review goals about refrigerant selection and choose equipment that meets the organization’s refrigerant goals (see Step 2). 9 https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/documents/ConstrAndDemo_EquipDisposal.pdf 8 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Take Action In Step 5, evaluate the current situation to determine whether it meets the goals identified in previous steps. This step also contains information to help develop a plan that will help meet the refrigerant goals set in Step 2. How can you verify equipment is working properly? Work with manufacturers to create a checklist for checking and maintaining equipment. Set up a schedule for checking and maintaining equipment. Identify personnel to execute checklist. Do you have equipment that is always problematic (requiring refrigerant to be added every year, for example)? Are there systems in the portfolio that are more likely to leak or have recurring leaks or failures?
